content: The references provided include a variety of studies examining the relationship between housing conditions, household crowding, and health outcomes. These studies explore the impact of housing on physical and mental health, with a focus on specific populations such as Inuit children, low-income women, and Indigenous communities. 1. Kohen DE, Bougie E, Guèvremont A (2015) investigated the relationship between housing conditions and health outcomes among Inuit children. Their findings highlighted the significant role of housing quality in influencing the health and well-being of this vulnerable population. 2. Pierse N, Carter K, Bierre S, Law D, Howden-Chapman P (2016) analyzed the effects of housing tenure, household crowding, and housing affordability on psychological distress using longitudinal data. Their study demonstrated that poor housing conditions exacerbate mental health challenges. 3. Regoeczi WC (2008) examined how men and women respond differently to high-density living environments. The study revealed gender-specific variations in coping mechanisms and psychological impacts associated with crowded housing. 4. Riva M, Larsen CVL, Bjerregaard P (2014a) explored the association between household crowding and psychosocial health among Inuit populations in Greenland. The study underscored the adverse effects of overcrowded living conditions on mental health. 5. Riva M, Plusquellec P, Juster RP, Laouan-Sidi EA, Abdous B, Lucas M, et al. (2014b) found that household crowding is linked to higher allostatic load among Inuit populations. This physiological stress marker indicates the cumulative burden of chronic stress due to poor living conditions. 6. Waters SF, Boyce WT, Eskenazi B, Alkon A (2016) studied the combined impact of maternal depression and overcrowded housing on the autonomic nervous system reactivity and externalizing behavior problems in vulnerable Latino children. Their findings highlighted the compounded risks of poor housing and maternal mental health on child development. 7. Wells NM, Harris JD (2007) conducted a longitudinal study on low-income women, showing that housing quality influences psychological distress, with social withdrawal acting as a mediating factor. Poor housing conditions were found to contribute to mental health challenges over time. 8. Chambers EC, Pichardo MS, Rosenbaum E (2016) investigated the relationship between sleep quality and the housing and neighborhood environment of urban Latino adults living in low-income housing. The study identified significant links between poor housing conditions and sleep disturbances. 9. Johnson DA, Drake C, Joseph CLM, Krajenta R, Hudgel DW, Cassidy-Bushrow AE (2015) examined the influence of neighborhood-level crowding on the severity of sleep-disordered breathing, mediated by body size. Their findings emphasized the role of environmental factors in sleep health. 10. Van der Spuy I, Karunanayake CP, Dosman JA, McMullin K, Zhao G, Abonyi S, et al. (2017) identified determinants of excessive daytime sleepiness in two First Nation communities. The study highlighted the role of housing and environmental factors in sleep-related health outcomes. These studies collectively emphasize the critical role of housing conditions, including crowding, affordability, and quality, in shaping physical and mental health outcomes across diverse populations. They also highlight the need for targeted interventions to address housing-related health disparities.
